q: Network Watcher is a:
opts: Regional service for monitoring and diagnosing network conditions in Azure IaaS
Global service for filtering and inspecting network traffic in Azure IaaS
exp: Network Watcher is a regional set of tools for monitoring and diagnosing network problems in Azure IaaS — IP flow verify, next hop, connection troubleshoot, packet capture, flow logs and more. It isn't a DNS service, a firewall or a load balancer; it only observes and tests.

q: By default, which resource group are Network Watcher instances created in?
exp: When Network Watcher is enabled automatically for a region, Azure creates its instance in a resource group called NetworkWatcherRG. It doesn't go into the VNet's resource group or 'DefaultResourceGroup'. You can create it elsewhere yourself if you enable it manually.

q: IP flow verify reports 'Access denied' with rule name 'DenyAllInBound'. What does that mean?
opts: No custom NSG rule allows the flow, so the default deny matched
Routing failed, so the packet was dropped before any NSG rule
exp: DenyAllInBound is one of the default NSG rules, with the lowest priority (65500). If it's the rule that matched, no higher-priority rule — including any custom rule you created — allowed the traffic. The fix is an allow rule with a lower priority number. A custom deny rule would show its own name.

q: Next hop returns 'None' for traffic from VM1 to 10.5.0.4. What does it mean?
opts: A route with next hop None (or no matching route) drops the traffic
The traffic goes to the internet, because no route in Azure matches it
exp: A next hop of None means Azure drops the traffic: either a route with next hop type None matches the destination, or no route matches at all. The traffic doesn't go to the internet, an NVA or peering — those would show as Internet, VirtualAppliance or VNetPeering.

q: Next hop reports 'VirtualAppliance 10.0.1.4' for traffic to the internet. What does it tell you?
opts: A UDR forces the traffic through the NVA at 10.0.1.4
An NSG rule redirects the traffic to the host 10.0.1.4
exp: A next hop type of VirtualAppliance with IP 10.0.1.4 means a user-defined route sends this traffic to the network virtual appliance at that address, and next hop also tells you which route table holds the route. Next hop is about routing only, so it says nothing about NSGs or DNS.

q: A packet capture must stop automatically after 10 minutes or 1 GB. Is that configurable?
opts: Yes — capture time limit, bytes per packet, and total size are configurable, with filters
No — every capture runs until you stop it manually, and only the filters can be set
exp: When you start a packet capture you can set a time limit, the maximum total size, the bytes captured per packet, and filters (protocol, IPs and ports). The capture stops when it reaches any of these limits, so 10 minutes or 1 GB is easy to configure.

q: Packet capture must start automatically when a VM's network metric crosses a threshold. How?
opts: An alert triggers an Azure Function or Automation runbook that starts a Network Watcher packet capture
A flow log with Traffic Analytics enabled starts a Network Watcher packet capture by itself
exp: Packet capture doesn't start on its own. To trigger it automatically, create an alert on the metric whose action group runs an Azure Function or Automation runbook that calls Network Watcher to start the capture. Flow logs only record flow summaries, and Advisor gives recommendations.

q: Connection troubleshoot reports 'Unreachable' with a hop showing 'NSG rule blocked'. What's next?
opts: Review effective security rules and adjust the NSG rule shown
Restart the destination VM and run the Connection troubleshoot again
exp: Connection troubleshoot has found that an NSG rule is blocking the path and shows which rule. Next, review the effective security rules on that NIC or subnet and change or add a rule to allow the traffic. Restarting the VM, changing disks or deleting the VNet doesn't affect NSG rules.

q: Where does Connection Monitor store its results for analysis and alerting?
exp: Connection Monitor stores its test results in a Log Analytics workspace, where you can query them with KQL. It also publishes metrics (such as round-trip time and checks failed %) that you can use in alerts. It doesn't use the Activity log or Key Vault for results.

q: Connection Monitor must test from an on-premises server to an Azure VM. What's needed on the on-premises server?
opts: An Azure Arc-enabled server with the Azure Monitor Agent (or a supported monitoring agent)
The Network Watcher VM extension, plus a public IP and an inbound NSG rule
exp: Connection Monitor needs an agent on non-Azure sources. For an on-premises server, onboard it to Azure Arc and install the Azure Monitor Agent so it can run the tests. The Network Watcher VM extension is for Azure VMs only, and a public IP alone doesn't run tests.

q: In Connection Monitor, what's a test group?
opts: A set of sources, destinations, and test configurations (protocol, port, frequency) evaluated together
A resource group that holds the sources and destinations, with one action group for their alerts
exp: A test group in Connection Monitor combines sources, destinations and test configurations (protocol, port, test frequency and thresholds), and all its tests are evaluated together. It isn't a resource group, an action group or an NSG.

q: You need an alert when latency between two VMs exceeds 50 ms over time. Which tool?
opts: Connection Monitor with a metric alert on round-trip time
IP flow verify scheduled every minute with a log alert
exp: Connection Monitor continuously measures round-trip time and checks failed between endpoints, and you can create a metric alert when round-trip time goes over 50 ms. IP flow verify, next hop and topology are one-off checks that don't measure latency over time.

q: What information does a flow log record contain?
opts: Source/destination IP and port, protocol, allowed or denied, and bytes/packets
Full packet payloads, TLS certificates, DNS queries, and the process name
exp: Flow logs record metadata about each flow: source and destination IP and port, protocol, direction, whether the traffic was allowed or denied, and (in version 2) bytes and packets. They never contain packet contents — use packet capture for that. They don't record DNS queries or CPU usage.

q: Which feature identifies top talkers, malicious IPs, and traffic hotspots from flow logs?
exp: Traffic Analytics processes flow logs in a Log Analytics workspace and adds geography and threat intelligence, so it can show top talkers, traffic hotspots, malicious IPs and open ports. Packet capture records raw packets, IP flow verify tests one flow, and VM insights monitors VMs.

q: Which processing interval options does Traffic Analytics offer?
opts: Once every day or once every week
exp: Traffic Analytics processes flow log data every 60 minutes by default, or every 10 minutes for faster insights (at a higher cost). It doesn't process every second, daily or weekly.

q: Which TWO Network Watcher tools help with NSG problems?
exp: IP flow verify tells you whether a specific flow is allowed or denied and which NSG rule decided. Effective security rules show the combined rules from every NSG applied to a NIC (subnet NSG plus NIC NSG). VPN troubleshoot checks gateways, and packet capture records traffic without explaining rules.

q: A VM can't reach a web server. Order a sensible Network Watcher diagnosis:
items: Check Next hop for the routing path
Run Connection troubleshoot to the destination
Run IP flow verify to check NSG rules
Run a packet capture if the issue is still unclear
exp: Start with Connection troubleshoot to confirm the problem and see where the path fails. Then use IP flow verify to check NSG rules, and next hop to check routing. Only if it's still unclear, run a packet capture to look at the actual traffic, which takes the most effort to analyse.

q: Answer Yes or No:
stmts: VPN troubleshoot can diagnose a virtual network gateway and its connections
IP flow verify works for traffic between two PaaS services
Network Watcher must exist in the region of the resources you diagnose
exp: VPN troubleshoot diagnoses a virtual network gateway and its connections. IP flow verify works on VM NICs, not traffic between two PaaS services. Topology shows network resources and doesn't need a running VM. Network Watcher must be enabled in the region of the resources you diagnose.

q: Which CLI command creates a Recovery Services vault?
opts: az backup vault create -g RG1 -n rsv1 -l westeurope
az recovery vault create -g RG1 -n rsv1 --region westeurope
exp: az backup vault create creates a Recovery Services vault, with -g, -n and -l (location). The other commands don't exist. Remember that VM backups need the vault to be in the same region as the VMs.

q: Which CLI command enables backup for VM1 with the DefaultPolicy?
opts: az backup protection enable-for-vm -g RG1 -v rsv1 --vm VM1 --policy-name DefaultPolicy
az backup vm add-protection -g RG1 --target-vault rsv1 --name VM1 --default-policy true
exp: az backup protection enable-for-vm associates a VM with a backup policy in a vault: -v is the vault, --vm the VM and --policy-name the policy (DefaultPolicy here). The first backup then runs on the policy's schedule. The other commands don't exist.

q: Which CLI command triggers an on-demand backup?
exp: az backup protection backup-now takes an on-demand backup of a protected item outside the schedule, and --retain-until sets how long that recovery point is kept. The other commands don't exist.

q: Which vault security feature requires a second user's approval (via Resource Guard) before critical operations like stopping protection and deleting backup data?
exp: Multi-user authorization (MUA) uses a Resource Guard, usually owned by a different team or tenant, so critical vault operations — such as deleting backup data or reducing retention — need that second person's approval. Soft delete keeps deleted data for 14 days, immutability blocks early deletion, and private endpoints secure network access.

q: Which vault setting prevents anyone from deleting recovery points before they expire, even admins (against ransomware)?
exp: An immutable vault blocks operations that could lose backup data, such as deleting recovery points before they expire or reducing retention. Once locked, immutability can't be turned off, even by admins, which protects against ransomware. Soft delete can be undone, and CRR and GRS are about redundancy.

q: Which roles let a user manage backups but NOT delete the vault or grant access?
exp: Backup Contributor can create and manage backups and restores, but can't delete the vault or give other users access. Owner can do everything, including granting access, User Access Administrator manages access, and Reader can only view.

q: Can you move a Recovery Services vault to another subscription?
opts: Yes, vault moves across resource groups and subscriptions are supported
Only if the vault is empty and was created with LRS redundancy
exp: You can move a Recovery Services vault to another resource group or subscription, but some limits apply — for example, you can't move it to another region, and some workloads have conditions. So it isn't 'never', and the vault doesn't have to be empty.

q: Backup data must be encrypted with your own key in the vault. What do you configure?
opts: Customer-managed keys for the Recovery Services vault
Infrastructure encryption on the cache storage account
exp: A Recovery Services vault can encrypt backup data with a customer-managed key stored in Key Vault, which the vault reads through its managed identity. Set this up before you protect items in the vault. Storage encryption settings and Azure Disk Encryption don't change how the vault encrypts its own data.

q: Which extension does Azure Backup install on a VM?
opts: Dependency agent with the AMA extension
exp: Azure VM backup installs the VMSnapshot extension (VMSnapshotLinux on Linux) through the VM agent to take snapshots. The MARS agent isn't used for whole Azure VM backups — it's for files and folders. The Dependency agent is for VM insights, and the ADE extension handles disk encryption.

q: What consistency does Azure Backup aim for with Windows VMs running VSS-aware apps?
exp: On Windows, Azure Backup uses the Volume Shadow Copy Service (VSS) to take application-consistent snapshots, so apps such as SQL Server are in a consistent state. On Linux you add pre- and post-scripts for the same effect. Crash-consistent is the fallback, not the goal.

q: An Azure VM's backup is crash-consistent instead of application-consistent. A likely reason?
opts: The VM was shut down during backup, or VSS failed
The vault uses GRS, or the VM has Premium SSD
exp: If the VM was shut down during the backup, or VSS failed (for example because of a VSS writer error), Azure Backup can only take a crash-consistent snapshot. Vault redundancy, disk type and tags don't affect consistency.

q: Is the first VM backup full or incremental?
opts: Full, and so is every later backup
exp: The first backup of a VM copies all the data (full). Every backup after that is incremental: only the blocks that changed since the last backup are transferred and stored, which saves time and storage. It isn't always full, always incremental from the start, or differential.

q: Which policy type is required for Trusted Launch VMs and supports hourly backups?
exp: The Enhanced VM backup policy is required for Trusted Launch VMs and other newer features. It supports several backups a day (every 4, 6, 8 or 12 hours), longer instant-restore retention, and zone-resilient snapshots. The Standard policy only does one backup a day. MARS and archive policies don't exist for this.

q: A VM has 4 data disks, but only the OS disk and disk 1 need protection. Is that possible?
opts: Yes — selective disk backup lets you exclude disks
No — a VM backup always includes all disks
exp: Selective disk backup lets you choose which data disks to include (the OS disk is always included), so you can protect only the OS disk and disk 1 and pay less. It works for Windows and Linux and doesn't need MARS.

q: Long-term monthly and yearly VM recovery points should move to a cheaper tier automatically. Which feature?
exp: Azure Backup has its own archive tier: eligible long-term recovery points (monthly and yearly) can move there automatically through the backup policy, or when Azure recommends it, and cost much less. Blob lifecycle rules work on blobs you own, not on backup data, and soft delete and immutability don't change tiers.

q: From where can you enable backup for a VM?
opts: From the VM's Backup blade or from the vault
From Azure Advisor or the Activity log
exp: You can enable backup from the VM itself (its Backup blade) or from the vault (Backup → Azure virtual machine). Both give the same result, and you can also use CLI, PowerShell or Azure Policy. It isn't limited to one entry point.

q: You restore a VM with the 'Create new VM' option. What's required?
opts: A target resource group and a VNet/subnet
A new vault in the target VNet's region
exp: 'Create new VM' needs to know where to put the restored VM — a target resource group, VNet and subnet — and, for some restores, a staging storage account in the same region. You don't need a new vault, and the VM is restored in the same region unless you use cross-region restore.

q: Which restore option keeps the existing VM's configuration (NICs, IP) and swaps only the disks to a recovery point?
exp: 'Replace existing' keeps the VM, with its NICs, IP and configuration, and swaps its disks for the ones from the recovery point. Azure takes a snapshot of the current disks first, so you can go back. 'Create new VM' makes another VM, and 'Restore disks' only creates disks.

q: You need a VM restored with custom settings (different size, extra NIC) using a template. Which option?
opts: Restore disks, then use the generated template to customize and deploy
Replace existing disks, then resize the VM and attach the extra NIC
exp: 'Restore disks' creates the disks plus a template for the VM. You can edit the template — for example a different size or an extra NIC — and deploy it. 'Create new VM' and 'Replace existing' use fixed settings, and file recovery only restores files.

q: After you run the file recovery script, how long does the recovery point stay mounted by default?
opts: 7 days (then the script must run again)
exp: After you run the file recovery script, the recovery point stays mounted as drives for 12 hours, then unmounts automatically. You can unmount it earlier from the portal once you've copied the files.

q: SQL Server in an Azure VM needs log backups every 15 minutes with point-in-time restore. Which solution?
opts: Azure Backup for SQL Server in Azure VMs
VM backup with the Enhanced policy
exp: Azure Backup for SQL Server in Azure VMs is a workload-aware backup in a Recovery Services vault. It supports full and differential backups plus log backups as often as every 15 minutes, so you can restore to a specific point in time. VM-level backup can't restore a database to a point in time, and MARS backs up files.

q: What's needed to register an on-premises server's MARS agent to a vault?
opts: Vault credentials file downloaded from the vault
A SAS token generated on the vault's storage
exp: Download a vault credentials file from the vault (it's valid for a limited time, usually 10 days) and use it during MARS setup to register the server with that vault. You also set an encryption passphrase. SSH keys, SAS tokens and Entra licences aren't used.

q: During MARS setup, you set an encryption passphrase. What happens if it's lost?
opts: Microsoft can't recover it, so you can't restore the data
Microsoft resets it after it verifies the subscription owner
exp: The MARS passphrase encrypts your backups before they leave the server, and Microsoft never sees it. If you lose it, nobody can decrypt the backups, so you can't restore. Store it safely, for example in Azure Key Vault.

q: On-premises Hyper-V VMs and SQL Server need app-aware backups to Azure. Which solution?
opts: Microsoft Azure Backup Server (MABS) or System Center DPM, with the vault as offsite storage
The MARS agent on each Hyper-V host, with app-aware mode enabled and the vault as storage
exp: Microsoft Azure Backup Server (MABS) or System Center DPM back up on-premises apps such as Hyper-V VMs and SQL Server in an application-aware way to local disk first, then send copies to a Recovery Services vault for offsite storage. MARS only backs up files, ASR is disaster recovery, and AzCopy just copies data.

q: Managed disks need backups several times a day with snapshot-based restore, without the VM backup extension. Which solution?
opts: Azure Disk Backup in a Backup vault
exp: Azure Disk Backup, configured in a Backup vault, takes incremental snapshots of managed disks without an agent or extension, several times a day if needed, and restores from those snapshots. The Recovery Services VM backup uses the VM extension, MARS is for files, and blob versioning is for blobs.

q: Which Azure Backup option protects blobs with continuous point-in-time recovery locally in the storage account (no vault copy)?
exp: Operational backup for Azure Blobs keeps the data in the storage account itself, using features such as point-in-time restore, versioning and soft delete, so you can restore continuously to any point. Vaulted backup copies blobs to a Backup vault. MARS and VM backup don't protect blobs.

q: Backup reports (usage, jobs, policies across vaults) require what?
opts: Diagnostic settings on the vaults sending data to a Log Analytics workspace
A storage account per vault and the Reports Reader role on each of them
exp: Backup reports are built on data in Log Analytics, so each vault needs a diagnostic setting that sends its backup data to a workspace. The reports then show jobs, usage and policies across vaults. Without that, the reports have nothing to show.

q: You want email notifications when backup jobs fail, using the recommended Azure Monitor approach. Use:
opts: Azure Monitor-based built-in alerts for Backup, routed with alert processing rules and action groups
Classic vault email notifications, sent to the co-administrators listed in the vault's properties
exp: Azure Backup now raises built-in alerts in Azure Monitor (for example for failed backup jobs). You route them to people with an alert processing rule plus an action group. Classic vault email alerts are being retired, and Advisor and budgets don't report job failures.

q: Where can you see the status of backup jobs (completed, failed, in progress) for a vault?
exp: Each vault has a Backup jobs page showing completed, failed and running jobs, and Resiliency (Azure Business Continuity Center) shows jobs across all vaults. The Activity log shows Azure operations, not job details, and metrics and VM insights don't track backup jobs.

q: Which TWO can a VM backup policy define?
exp: A VM backup policy defines the schedule — when and how often backups run — and retention: how long daily, weekly, monthly and yearly recovery points are kept. It doesn't define the VM's size after restore or any NSG rules.

q: You change a backup policy's daily retention from 30 to 10 days. What happens to existing recovery points?
opts: Existing points follow the new retention, so points older than 10 days are cleaned up
Existing points keep the old 30 days, and only new points follow the 10-day retention
Nothing; only new VMs are affected
exp: Changing retention in a backup policy applies to existing recovery points too. When daily retention drops from 30 to 10 days, points older than 10 days are cleaned up (unless they're also kept as weekly, monthly or yearly points). So check the effect before you shorten retention.

ctx: Vault RSV1 (West Europe, GRS, CRR enabled, soft delete on) protects VM1 (West Europe) with a Standard daily policy: 30 daily, 12 monthly.
q: Answer Yes or No:
stmts: VM1 can be restored in North Europe (the paired region) at any time
RSV1 can also protect VM2 located in East US
If someone stops protection and deletes the data, it can be recovered within 14 days
You can still change RSV1 to LRS because VM1 is already protected
exp: With GRS and cross-region restore, VM1 can be restored in the paired region (North Europe) at any time. The vault can only protect VMs in its own region, so not VM2 in East US. Soft delete keeps deleted backup data for 14 days. Redundancy is locked once the first item is protected, so RSV1 can't be changed to LRS now.
